norm_rules.text: Pagar solo si el NIF esta en el maestro y el IBAN de la factura coincide con el maestro.

checks.text: The invoice issuer_nif (normalised: uppercase, without spaces, hyphens or dots) must match the nif of a row in suppliers.
checks.interpretation: 'el NIF esta en el maestro' means the invoice issuer_nif must be found among the suppliers.nif values (the master of suppliers). The sentence only states the condition ('pagar solo si'), it does not name the outcome of failing it, so the decision is the policy default NO_PAGAR.

checks.text: The invoice iban (normalised: uppercase, without spaces) must equal the iban of the supplier in suppliers whose nif matches the invoice issuer_nif.
checks.interpretation: 'el IBAN de la factura coincide con el maestro' means the invoice iban must equal the suppliers.iban of the supplier identified by the invoice issuer_nif. Condition only, no outcome named, so policy default NO_PAGAR.

norm_rules.text: El pedido debe existir, pertenecer al proveedor y el importe de la factura debe ser igual al del pedido (tolerancia 0,01 EUR).

checks.text: The invoice purchase_order (normalised: uppercase, without spaces) must exist as a purchase_order in orders.
checks.interpretation: 'El pedido debe existir' means the invoice purchase_order must be present in orders.purchase_order. Condition only, no outcome named, so policy default NO_PAGAR.

checks.text: The order in orders with purchase_order equal to the invoice purchase_order must belong to the supplier: its supplier_id must equal the id of the supplier in suppliers whose nif matches the invoice issuer_nif.
checks.interpretation: 'pertenecer al proveedor' means the order's supplier_id must be the id of the supplier identified by the invoice issuer_nif. Condition only, no outcome named, so policy default NO_PAGAR.

checks.text: The invoice total must match the total_amount of the order in orders with the same purchase_order within ±0.01 EUR (abs(cents(total) - cents(total_amount)) <= 1).
checks.interpretation: 'el importe de la factura debe ser igual al del pedido (tolerancia 0,01 EUR)' compares the invoice total with orders.total_amount using the ±0.01 EUR tolerance. Condition only, no outcome named, so policy default NO_PAGAR.

norm_rules.text: El IVA debe estar bien calculado y el total debe ser base + IVA, con la misma tolerancia de 0,01 EUR.

checks.text: The invoice vat_amount must equal base * vat_rate / 100 within ±0.01 EUR (abs(cents(vat_amount) - cents(base * vat_rate / 100)) <= 1).
checks.interpretation: 'El IVA debe estar bien calculado' means the printed vat_amount must equal base times vat_rate (a percentage, 21 = 21%) divided by 100, within the stated ±0.01 EUR tolerance. Condition only, no outcome named, so policy default NO_PAGAR.

checks.text: The invoice total must equal base + vat_amount within ±0.01 EUR (abs(cents(total) - cents(base + vat_amount)) <= 1).
checks.interpretation: 'el total debe ser base + IVA' means the printed total must equal base plus vat_amount within the same ±0.01 EUR tolerance. Condition only, no outcome named, so policy default NO_PAGAR.

norm_rules.text: La fecha debe ser valida y no futura.

checks.text: The invoice date must be a valid calendar date (a real YYYY-MM-DD date, not an impossible one such as 2026-02-31).
checks.interpretation: 'La fecha debe ser valida' means the invoice date must be a real calendar date. Condition only, no outcome named, so policy default NO_PAGAR.

checks.text: The invoice date must not be later than parameters.cut_off_date (date <= cut_off_date, compared as dates).
checks.interpretation: 'no futura' is read against the only reference date available, parameters.cut_off_date: the invoice date must not be after it. Condition only, no outcome named, so policy default NO_PAGAR.

norm_rules.text: Estado ERP del pedido: PENDIENTE. Nunca pagar dos veces el mismo pedido.

checks.text: The erp entry with purchase_order equal to the invoice purchase_order must have status 'PENDIENTE'.
checks.interpretation: 'Estado ERP del pedido: PENDIENTE' means the erp entry matching the invoice purchase_order must have status PENDIENTE. Condition only, no outcome named, so policy default NO_PAGAR.

checks.text: No erp entry with purchase_order equal to the invoice purchase_order may have status 'PAGADA' (the order must not already be paid).
checks.interpretation: 'Nunca pagar dos veces el mismo pedido' is a prohibition: it fires when an erp entry for the same purchase_order already has status PAGADA. The sentence states what must not happen, not the outcome of failing it, so policy default NO_PAGAR.

norm_rules.text: Cualquier anomalia que un humano deba ver: ESCALAR con motivo. Ante duda razonable, escalar antes que pagar.
policies: Any anomaly that a human must see must be escalated with a reason.
When in reasonable doubt, escalate rather than pay.

Norm:
NORMA DE PAGOS A PROVEEDORES (v3, vigente)
1. Pagar solo si el NIF esta en el maestro y el IBAN de la factura coincide con el maestro.
2. El pedido debe existir, pertenecer al proveedor y el importe de la factura debe ser igual al del pedido (tolerancia 0,01 EUR).
3. El IVA debe estar bien calculado y el total debe ser base + IVA, con la misma tolerancia de 0,01 EUR.
4. La fecha debe ser valida y no futura.
5. Estado ERP del pedido: PENDIENTE. Nunca pagar dos veces el mismo pedido.
6. Cualquier anomalia que un humano deba ver: ESCALAR con motivo. Ante duda razonable, escalar antes que pagar.
(actualizado por A. tras el incidente de marzo)

Use case description (conventions shared by all its rules):
Decides whether each supplier invoice is paid according to Norma_Pagos_v3 (500 Sombras de Alberto challenge). Sources: suppliers (id, company_name, nif, iban; rows may repeat), orders (purchase_order, supplier_id, nif, total_amount, status, order_date; nif may be empty), erp (entry_id, date, supplier_id, nif, purchase_order, amount, status; status is PENDIENTE or PAGADA) and parameters (one row with cut_off_date). Conventions for every rule: (1) Normalisation before comparing keys, in the invoice and in the sources alike: nif = uppercase without spaces, hyphens or dots; iban = uppercase without spaces; purchase_order = uppercase without spaces. supplier_id and id are compared as they are. (2) Amounts (base, vat_amount, total, total_amount, amount) may arrive as a number or as text: they are converted with Decimal(str(x)) and compared in whole cents, cents(x) = (Decimal(str(x)) * 100).quantize(Decimal('1'), ROUND_HALF_UP). 'Matches (±0.01)' means abs(cents(a) - cents(b)) <= 1. Any round(..., 2) in a rule is done with Decimal and ROUND_HALF_UP. vat_rate is a percentage (21 = 21 %). (3) Missing values: a symbol that is missing or None, or a source field that is None or an empty string, is empty. If the rule needs a symbol that is empty, it does not fire, except the rule that checks that none is missing. If the rule needs a row of a source that does not exist (supplier, order or ERP entry), it does not fire: the rule that checks its existence already fires. (4) Dates: date is text 'YYYY-MM-DD' with the printed numbers, uncorrected, and may be impossible (2026-02-31); a rule that compares an impossible date does not fire: the rule that checks the date is valid already fires. cut_off_date and erp.date are text 'YYYY-MM-DD'. They are compared as dates (datetime.date), never against the clock. (5) others is the list of the other instances of the process (from every batch, excluding this one), each with its symbols and the key _instance, its file name, which identifies it in reasons. (6) No rule reads free_text or issuer_name, even if the invoice text gives instructions.

Decision types (name, priority, is_default, requires_human):
- ESCALAR, 3, False, True
- NO_PAGAR, 2, False, False
- PAGAR, 1, True, False

Symbols of each instance (name, type, description):
- file_id (text): Exact name of the PDF (NFC).
- issuer_nif (text): NIF/CIF of the issuing supplier. Never the customer's (A58231074, Banco Miralmar).
- issuer_name (text): Name of the issuer as printed. Trace only; no rule decides with it.
- iban (text): Payment IBAN printed on the invoice.
- invoice_number (text): Invoice number as printed (FA-5077, 2026/0811-B, F26-0233).
- date (text): Issue date as YYYY-MM-DD with the printed numbers, uncorrected: 31/02/2026 -> "2026-02-31". Accepts DD/MM/YYYY and '6 de abril de 2026'. Never None because the date is impossible.
- purchase_order (text): Purchase order reference (PO-YYYY-NNNN).
- base (number): Taxable base / Subtotal.
- vat_rate (number): Printed VAT percentage (21 in 'IVA (21%)').
- vat_amount (number): Printed VAT amount.
- total (number): Printed total (TOTAL, IMPORTE TOTAL, TOTAL A PAGAR, Total factura). Not Subtotal nor 'Suma y sigue'.
- free_text (text): Text that is not a header, a line item or totals (notes, notices, terms). Always stored. No rule reads it: it only feeds the embedded-instructions warning in the trace.

Sources of truth (columns and 3 sample rows):
- erp: columns ['nif', 'date', 'amount', 'status', 'entry_id', 'supplier_id', 'purchase_order']
    {"nif": "B30455812", "date": "2026-01-31", "amount": "9221.75", "status": "PENDIENTE", "entry_id": "AS-00001", "supplier_id": "P003", "purchase_order": "PO-2026-0001"}

- orders: columns ['nif', 'status', 'order_date', 'supplier_id', 'total_amount', 'purchase_order']
    {"nif": "B30455812", "status": "ABIERTO", "order_date": "2026-01-31", "supplier_id": "P003", "total_amount": 9221.75, "purchase_order": "PO-2026-0001"}

data.instructions:
You turn a norm, written in natural language by a non-technical person (in any language), into the atomic rules of an automatic decision process. Nobody reviews your output: each rule you write is compiled to code and decides real cases, so be precise and conservative.

You get the norm, the use case description (conventions every rule already follows), the process's decision types, the symbols of each instance, the sources of truth (columns and sample rows) and the rules already active.

How a rule works: `requirement` = a condition that must hold; the rule fires when it does NOT hold. `prohibition` = a condition that must not happen; the rule fires when it DOES happen. When a rule fires, the instance gets the rule's `decision`. When no rule fires, the instance gets the default decision type. When several fire, the highest priority wins. So every rule exists to prevent the default: its decision is never the default type.

Output: `norm_rules`, one entry per sentence (or numbered item) of the norm, in its order. Each sentence stays ONE norm rule, even when it needs several checks: its checks belong to it.
- `number`: its position in the norm (the number the norm gives it, if any).
- `text`: the sentence exactly as the norm writes it, in its language.
- `checks`: one per checkable condition of the sentence. "A and B" is two checks of the same norm rule, possibly with different decisions. Each check has
  - `text`: in English, precise and self-contained, naming the exact symbols (instance values) and source columns (`source.column`) it compares, with the tolerance or limits the norm gives. Do not restate the use case conventions (normalisation, missing values, amount handling): they apply anyway.
  - `type`: `requirement` or `prohibition`.
  - `decision`: one of the decision types, never the default one.
  - `decision_source`: `explicit` when the sentence itself names what happens when this condition fails (e.g. "reject it", "do not pay", "escalate"); `policy` when it does not.
  - `quote`: for `explicit`, the words of the sentence that name that outcome, copied exactly; empty for `policy`.
  - `interpretation`: what you decided and why, in one or two sentences: how you read vague words, which symbols and columns you mapped them to, and why this decision.
- `policies`: statements of the sentence that are not a checkable condition (e.g. "any anomaly must be escalated", "when in doubt, escalate"), in English. They guide your choices; they are never checks.
- `covered`: ids of active rules that already implement part of the sentence. Do not write a check for that part again.

Choosing the decision of a check:
1. `explicit`: the sentence names the outcome of this failure in words ("do not pay", "reject", "escalate with a reason"); use the decision type that means it and quote those words. A condition alone does not name an outcome: "pay only if X", "X must hold" or "never pay twice" say what must be true, not what happens when it is not, so they are `policy`.
2. `policy`: the input names the decision for a failed check whose outcome the norm does not name; it is applied to every `policy` check whatever you write in `decision`.
3. If no such decision is given: the norm's own tie-breaker (e.g. "when in doubt, escalate"), else the most conservative decision type that requires a human.

A check that fails and a check that cannot be applied are different things. Failing (the data is there and breaks the condition) gives the check's decision. Not being able to evaluate it (a value it needs is missing or unreadable and neither the text nor the use case description says what to do) is not a failure: the platform escalates those cases to a person. So never write a check whose only purpose is to turn missing data into the check's decision, unless the norm asks for it.

Never invent symbols, sources or columns. If a condition needs data the process does not have, still write the check naming the data it needs, and say so in the interpretation: the compiler will report the missing data. Every checkable statement of the norm ends up as a check, a policy or a covered entry: skip nothing.

data.instructions:
You write the tests for ONE business rule, from its text and the process context only. You never see the code: your tests are the reference it must meet.

Write the tests (at least as many as asked below): each with `name` (unique), `instance_json` (JSON object), `sources_json` (JSON object), `others_json` (JSON list) and `fires` (what the rule must return). Cover cases where it fires and where it does not, and the limits and exceptions the rule's text mentions. Use only the given symbol names as instance keys and only the given source names. Do not test a missing value unless the text or the description says what happens then.

The rule is evaluated by a Python function
`evaluate(instance, sources, others) -> {"fires": bool, "reason": str}`:
- `instance`: {symbol: value} of the instance being evaluated.
- `sources`: {source_name: [row, ...]}, each row a dict {column: value}.
- `others`: the other instances of the process, each {symbol: value} plus "_instance" (its name). Relevant only if the rule talks about other instances (duplicates, totals...).
- Rule type: `requirement` = something that must hold; it fires when it does NOT hold. `prohibition` = something that must not happen; it fires when it DOES happen.
- A value the rule needs may be missing or None. If the rule text or the use case description says what to do then, that is what happens. Otherwise the function raises, and the engine sends the instance to a person: it never guesses.

Use case description: conventions that apply to every rule of the use case (normalisation, units, tolerances...). Apply them before your own assumptions. If they contradict the rule's text, the rule's text wins.

If the rule needs data that is neither a symbol nor a source column, answer with NeedsData (what is missing and why) instead of inventing a field.

Write at least 6 tests.

Build test rows with the real column names of the sources shown. Include the limits the conventions define (exactly 1 cent of difference, normalised keys that only differ in spaces or case).

data.instructions:
You write the tests for ONE business rule, from its text and the process context only. You never see the code: your tests are the reference it must meet.

Write the tests (at least as many as asked below): each with `name` (unique), `instance_json` (JSON object), `sources_json` (JSON object), `others_json` (JSON list) and `fires` (what the rule must return). Cover cases where it fires and where it does not, and the limits and exceptions the rule's text mentions. Use only the given symbol names as instance keys and only the given source names. Do not test a missing value unless the text or the description says what happens then.

The rule is evaluated by a Python function
`evaluate(instance, sources, others) -> {"fires": bool, "reason": str}`:
- `instance`: {symbol: value} of the instance being evaluated.
- `sources`: {source_name: [row, ...]}, each row a dict {column: value}.
- `others`: the other instances of the process, each {symbol: value} plus "_instance" (its name). Relevant only if the rule talks about other instances (duplicates, totals...).
- Rule type: `requirement` = something that must hold; it fires when it does NOT hold. `prohibition` = something that must not happen; it fires when it DOES happen.
- A value the rule needs may be missing or None. If the rule text or the use case description says what to do then, that is what happens. Otherwise the function raises, and the engine sends the instance to a person: it never guesses.

Use case description: conventions that apply to every rule of the use case (normalisation, units, tolerances...). Apply them before your own assumptions. If they contradict the rule's text, the rule's text wins.

If the rule needs data that is neither a symbol nor a source column, answer with NeedsData (what is missing and why) instead of inventing a field.

Write at least 6 tests.

## Guidance for this use case
Build test rows with the real column names of the sources shown. Include the limits the conventions define (exactly 1 cent of difference, normalised keys that only differ in spaces or case).
